paper_title: HEP-Ex-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Performance in High Energy Physics Experiment Data Analyses with Sealed Worlds

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agentic systems are increasingly being explored for automating experimental high-energy physics measurements, but the correctness of their results can today be reliably evaluated only via extensive expert review. To address this, we propose a method to perform detailed quantitative evaluations of agent-driven analyses through the use of blind analysis and injection tests, which are critical in a typical expert review. Agents develop a data analysis pipeline on a public dataset, while the evaluation is performed on programmatically generated sealed private datasets where signals are injected and simulation settings varied within realistic detector uncertainties. By requiring agents to provide a single workflow that is evaluated across these "sealed worlds", we are able to test the accuracy and robustness of the workflows. We demonstrate the approach on four tasks built from CMS open data and present it as a way to reliably benchmark scientific work in experimental high-energy physics. At the time of writing, the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, reaches 60% of the score of the expert reference analyses on average, ahead of GPT 6 Astra at 38% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 31%. In individual sessions on one of the tasks, Gemini 4 Argon exceeds the reference. The benchmark is hosted at https://hep-ex-bench.github.io

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Scientific research is moving toward systems that execute parts of the process autonomously through artificial intelligence (AI) agents built on large language models (LLMs). In high-energy physics (HEP), agents can now carry out substantial parts of the elaborate data analysis pipeline, from event selection and background modeling to the construction of full likelihood [13]. The question is therefore no longer whether agents can analyze data, but how the quality and reliability of their analyses can be evaluated. An analysis that runs to completion is not necessarily correct. The true result on observed data is unknown, and an *Lead authors anovaka@mit.edu byiyang26@mit.edu cdolores.garcia@cern.ch demoreno@mit.edu ejkrupa@slac.stanford.edu fvbresopla@fas.harvard.edu gsambt@mit.edu hl.heinrich@tum.de imakagan@slac.stanford.edu jpcharris@mit.edu Figure 1: The sealed-world benchmarking scheme. The agent works from the task prompt and public world, and delivers pipeline. The pipeline is then frozen and rerun on sealed worlds with different hidden truths. The evaluator scores the results against the truths and against an expert reference analysis of the same worlds. The worlds are assembled beforehand from simulation with injected truths  (Fig. 3)  . agent that reproduces published measurement may simply have recalled or looked up the accepted value [4, 5]. Expert review does not scale, and language-model evaluation [6] can be exploited into accepting pipelines that would fail such review [7]. Benchmarks are therefore needed that have reproducible scoring methodology and are characteristic of real physics analyses, with truths isolated from the web and from training data. These benchmarks should evaluate both the precision of measurement and whether the analysis methods are correct. To address this gap we propose sealed-world benchmarking, which follows two established methods of experimental physics, blind analysis [8] and injection tests [9]. In blinded mode, the analysis is tested on pseudodata with known injected truth before the signal region of the observed data is analyzed. reliable analysis is one that recovers the injected truth within its quoted uncertainty [10]. In HEP-Ex-Bench, the High-Energy Physics Experiment Benchmark, we present mechanism for reliable evaluation 1 of AI agents through sealed-world injections. An agent develops an analysis once on public dataset (public world), built from simulated samples in the format of real analysis input; the agent then delivers pipeline that aims to produce unbiased physics results over wide range of physics outcomes and detector behaviors. The pipeline is frozen and executed in isolation on many varied sealed worlds. These sealed worlds are built with the full detector simulation of an experiment, here the open simulated data of the CMS experiment [11]. The sealed worlds differ in their parameters of interest1 and in their detector response, which are hidden from the agent. The evaluator harness scores the results against the hidden truths and against an expert reference analysis of the same worlds, and checks the method programmatically, for example the goodness of fit of the delivered model. Figure 1 shows the scheme. memorized value, fit tuned to the public world, or an understated uncertainty scores poorly on the sealed worlds. Higgs boson mass of 125 GeV, for example, is wrong in world where it is 115 GeV. In contrast, sound analysis recovers the truths with uncertainties consistent with the sealed-world variations. Section 2 reviews related work, and Sec. 3 defines the sealed-world evaluation, the failure modes it is designed to catch, and the score. Section 4 presents four example tasks, and Sec. 5 describes how their worlds are built from CMS simulation [1218]. Section 6 validates the expert reference analyses and the evaluator and reports campaign of agents, Sec. 7 discusses the results and the limits of the method, and Sec. 8 discusses implications and way forward for the field.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Recent work on AI agents has largely focused on the construction of agentic workflows. HEP-Ex-Bench addresses their evaluation. Evaluation can be performed against published value, hidden reference or an injected truth. The papers summarized below are grouped in that order, from the weakest to the strongest ground truth, and are compared in Table 1. The most direct evaluation of an agentic workflow checks its result against published results. PaperBench asks agents to replicate machine-learning papers, runs their code again and compares the agents with human experts [19], and PRBench scores how well agents reproduce the results of published physics papers [20]. In HEP, Gendreau-Distler et al. compare many language models on Higgs-boson analysis of ATLAS Open Data [2], Dr.Sai measures branching fractions on the full simulation of the BESIII experiment [3], and ColliderBench, the work closest to this paper in its tasks, asks agents to rebuild published LHC [21] searches and scores the signal yields that they predict [22]. published value, however, cannot reliably tell robust analysis apart from recalled one. Only Dr.Sai reports uncertainties, and it checks them through pulls (deviations from the truth in units of the reported uncertainty) on single simulated sample instead of scoring them. stronger evaluation compares the result with reference that the agent cannot see. MLE-bench scores machinelearning engineering against test sets that the agents do not see but that are derived from public data [23], HEPTABench evaluates agents repeatedly on HEP tasks with hidden reference values [24], and DiscoverPhysics asks agents to discover 1The quantities that an analysis sets out to measure, such as the Higgs boson mass. Lastly, evaluation can be performed against an injected truth, grading both the measured values and their uncertainties. The HEP data challenges, including HiggsML, the LHC Olympics and Dark Machines, and the HDR Gravitational Wave Anomaly Challenge, all construct evaluation methods for finding hidden signals in simulated collision events or gravitational wave data [2528]. FAIR Universe, the closest to this work in its scoring, runs every submitted model on pseudoexperiments with re-drawn signal strengths and systematic shifts, then scores the coverage and magnitude of the reported uncertainties [29]. These challenges, however, evaluate specific methods rather than agents that carry out complete analyses, and their data are precomputed features of single analysis, so the task is statistical inference alone. HEP-Ex-Bench combines the elements of these three groups  (Table 1)  . As in the first group, the agent develops whole analysis. As in FAIR Universe, the truths are hidden and re-drawn for every evaluation and the reported uncertainties are scored. In addition, the statistical model that the agent delivers is checked, for example for its goodness of fit, so an analysis is scored on its method as well as on its result.

sections.title: 3 Sealed-world evaluation
sections.content: Since the truth in experimentally collected data is unknown, an analysis in HEP is conventionally developed and calibrated on simulation, and tested with injected signals [10]. The application to the collected data is only performed once the method is fixed [8]. HEP-Ex-Bench extends this practice with sealed worlds, simulated datasets that emulate experimentally collected data and whose true values are chosen by the evaluator and hidden from the tested agent (their construction is described in Sec. 5.1). An analysis is tested on many sealed worlds, each with different injected truth, so that only 2 method that holds across these variations recovers the injected truths. The scheme applies to any measurement and is illustrated by four tasks (Sec. 4). An agent works on task in one development session, in this paper single run of at most 7.5 in sandbox. In it, the agent is given prompt in which the task is stated, the evaluation contract, in which the deliverables, output formats, and self-check are fixed while as little taskspecific information as possible is revealed (App. C.1), the public world pseudodata in the format of real analysis inputs, and Figure 2: Toy analyses that many sealed worlds expose: the reported Higgs boson mass mH against the injected one on nine worlds, with the expert reference analysis as open diamonds. the nominal simulation (with default detector settings). 3.2.1 Measurement The agent develops pipeline with web access to look up published methods. Once delivered, the pipeline is frozen and rerun offline, in isolation, on the sealed worlds  (Fig. 1)  . submission that breaks the contract is not evaluated.

sections.title: 3.1 Evaluation on many sealed worlds
sections.content: In every task, an analysis is scored by its results on many sealed worlds. Three ways in which an analysis can look right without being right are guarded against: Knowing the answer. value is recalled from the literature or from training data, or read from the truths, such as 125 GeV Higgs boson mass reported on every world where the mass is varied (Fig. 2, left). The sealed truths are drawn anew and are on no web page, and the isolated runs and the session transcripts are checked for access to them. Overfitting to the public world. An analysis is tuned on the one public dataset provided to the agent, and is right for that world but biased toward its value on the others (Fig. 2, center). The pipeline is frozen before it runs on any sealed world, and those worlds differ in their parameters of interest, background simulation, and detector response; only an analysis with full detector, background and signal variations will result in an unbiased result. Guessing. On single world, guess can agree with the truth, and sound analysis can miss it through fluctuation. The two are separated on many worlds, as shown by the toy study in App. B.8. Misstated uncertainties, bias shared by every world (Fig. 2, right) and unsound methods are caught by the score itself, through the scoring rule, the combination of the worlds and the quality terms (Sec. 3.2). The checks are verified with deliberately flawed and cheating submissions, whose scores are given in App. B.7.

sections.title: 4 Tasks
sections.content: The four tasks are based on analyses carried out in practice at the LHC, two measurements (fits) and two calibrations  (Table 3)  . Each requires the full chain of real analysis, from the calibration of the physics objects to statistical model with its systematic uncertainties, and each has an expert reference analysis that follows published CMS method (App. E). Table 3: The four tasks, their results and the appendices that describe them and their expert reference analyses. signal strength is production rate in units of the Standard Model (SM) prediction.

sections.title: 5 Datasets
sections.content: The worlds are built from CMS Open Data [1217, 32, 33], the simulation of protonproton collisions at = 13 TeV in the 2016 detector conditions, together with private signal simulation produced under the same conditions, both in MiniAOD (a reduced analysis format of CMS that keeps all reconstructed particles [34]). The Higgs-boson signal is generated with Pythia 8 [35] at varying masses, and its events are then simulated and reconstructed with the official CMS software [36], including additional protonproton interactions within the same or nearby bunch crossings (pileup) [18]. The detector, its coordinate system and the kinematic variables are described in Ref. [11]. For HIGGSWIDTH, off-shell production through gluon fusion and electroweak processes, with its interference with the ZZ continuum, is generated with MadGraph5_aMC@NLO [37] and passes the same simulation and reconstruction (App. D.3). The JETCALIB worlds are built from simulated DrellYan and multijet events of CMS Open Data [3846] in format that keeps all reconstructed particles. The public world of every task is released with the benchmark (see Code and data availability), while the sealed worlds used for the results are not. The worlds are indistinguishable from data in their format and carry no generator information. The results of HIGGSLEPMASS, HIGGSWIDTH, LEPCALIB and JETCALIB use 40, 30, 10 and 10 sealed worlds Figure 3: Production of the worlds. 4 of 50, 100, 10 and 1 fb12, respectively.

sections.title: 5.1 Detector response and signal injection
sections.content: The worlds differ from the nominal simulation in the detector response and in the injected signal, and some HIGGSWIDTH worlds also in the theory prediction. Each world has one of 13 detector profiles, the nominal one or one of twelve modified ones, applied to both its signal and its background. profile rescales the transverse momentum of every reconstructed particle by smooth function of pT and η, smears pT, η and ϕ, and changes the identification and trigger efficiencies by smooth data-to-simulation ratio. The exact functional forms and their parameters are withheld to prevent cheating. Jets and the missing transverse momentum [47] are rebuilt from the modified particles, so every event stays consistent (App. D). The signal of world is generated according to its parameters of interest, the Higgs-boson mass and the signal strength, or in HIGGSWIDTH the width and the on-shell signal strength, with the production and decay rates, the width and the acceptance changing consistently with the mass. world may contain no signal. The detector profiles and the signal injection act on all leptons, particle-flow candidates [34], jets and the missing transverse momentum alike, so worlds for other analyses or for the calibration of other physics objects can be produced consistently across different background processes and final states.

sections.title: 8 Conclusions and outlook
sections.content: We have presented the building blocks of HEP-Ex-Bench, benchmark for autonomous physics analysis. Anchoring the score to the expert reference analysis and to standard statistical tools provides an objective way of evaluating correctness, without expert review of every analysis and without language-model judge. The score separates accurate analyses from overconfident, biased or failing ones. As agents take on more of the analysis work, we argue that such quantitative and repeatable tests should become common practice in their evaluation. HEP-Ex-Bench can be extended to further kinds of analysis, such as calibrations of other physics objects and frontier measurements that need multivariate discriminants. Future tasks could also include other experiments, such as ATLAS, LHCb, neutrino detectors and gravitational waves. Building such tasks remains the work of human experts. Which analyses become tasks, which properties of the worlds vary and how strongly, and what correct analysis has to deliver are decisions of physics judgment, made once per task and then applied to every agent.

sections.content: C.1 Evaluation contract The evaluation contract of Sec. 3 fixes the following. Submission: directory whose pipeline produces result on world, in fixed software environment and within limits of time and memory. Parameters of interest: named signal strengths, cross sections, and masses and widths of the Higgs, and bosons and of the top quark. Nuisance parameters: named by source, the scale, resolution and efficiencies of the physics objects, pileup and theory. Likelihood-fit tasks: the statistical model in the HistFactory format [54, 55] with the selected events, and for mass also the likelihood on grid of fixed masses. Calibration tasks: the correction functions in the correctionlib format [56]. Self-check: script given to the agent runs the pipeline on the public world in the same way as the evaluation and checks the format of its outputs. C.2 Prompt tiers The prompts of all tasks share the same structure. The lowest tier, P0, just states the task and the output format. Each higher tier adds more guidance, such as the physics context, an ordered expert plan, or the sources of systematic uncertainty to evaluate, without specifying their size. No prompt tier mentions the expert reference analysis or states which detector effects vary between worlds. As an example, the three prompts of HIGGSLEPMASS are given in full below. In the CMS Open Data samples, DrellYan events are generated with MadGraph5_aMC@NLO [37], with jets merged in the MLM [59] or the FxFx [60] scheme, qq ZZ and top quark pair events with POWHEG [6163], gg ZZ events with MCFM [64], and multijet events with Pythia 8 [35]. (a) (b) D.3 Off-shell samples The off-shell samples of HIGGSWIDTH are generated at leading order with MadGraph5_aMC@NLO 3.6.7 [37]: gluon fusion, gg ZZ 4ℓ, loop induced and normalized with QCD correction that depends on the four-lepton mass, and electroweak production, qq 4ℓqq, at tree level. The Higgs-boson signal, the continuum and their sum with the interference are generated separately, and the width is changed through the couplings of the Higgs boson so that the on-shell rate stays fixed, as in the CMS off-shell measurement [67]. All samples are passed through the official CMS simulation of the 2016 conditions [18], and the agent receives them at the SM width only.

sections.title: E Tasks and expert reference analyses
sections.content: Each task has an expert reference analysis that sets the precision and wall time benchmarks for the model evaluation. It runs under the same contract as submission, on the same inputs and without access to the truth. Every reference recovers every injected truth without bias and with pulls of unit width, within the statistical resolving power of the worlds. E.1 HIGGSLEPMASS Task. HIGGSLEPMASS measures the mass mH of the Higgs boson and its signal strength µ in the decay ZZ 4ℓ channel, with ℓ = e, µ. The signal strength is defined as the production rate in units of the Standard Model (SM) prediction. The task requires lepton calibration, an estimate of the background from misidentified leptons, mass-dependent signal model, likelihood fit and systematic uncertainties. As in real experiment, the lepton response of world may differ from the nominal simulation and, left uncorrected, bias the extracted mass and signal strength. The leptons must therefore be calibrated with the ℓℓ events of the same world and the resulting calibration must be propagated to the four-lepton signal region. With its very small background, the four-lepton channel provides the tightest single-channel constraint on its mass, mH = 125.04 0.12 GeV with 138 fb1 of CMS Run-2 data [68]. The HIGGSLEPMASS reference follows the published CMS measurement with 35.9 fb1 of Run-2 data [69]. The HIGGSWIDTH worlds take six of the modified profiles, applied to the leptons when world is assembled. In JETCALIB, the detector effects are injected in the particles of the jets. The response to each kind of particle is modified and smeared, in some worlds as function of pT or η or only in one region of the detector, and the jets are clustered again. The jet response then depends on the composition, the pT and the η of the jet, as it does in data. In HIGGSLEPMASS and HIGGSWIDTH, the DrellYan events are complemented with samples binned in the number of jets [32] and in the scalar sum of the jet transverse momenta [33], and in HIGGSWIDTH the gg ZZ continuum is part of 18 cludes only worlds containing Higgs signal. With the on-shell rate fixed, the off-shell signal grows with µonξ and its interference with the gg ZZ and electroweak ZZ continuum with µonξ. The task requires an analysis with lepton calibration, joint fit of the on-shell peak and the off-shell spectrum, kinematic discriminant against the continuum, from which the signal differs only in its kinematics, and prediction at any width built from simulation at the SM width alone. Lepton calibration. The momentum scale and resolution of each flavor are measured on ℓℓ events. The simulated leptons are scaled and smeared in categories of pT and η of the two leptons, and the dilepton mass templates are fitted to the pseudodata, with the procedure repeated until the corrections are stable. The angular resolutions are fitted in the same events, from the width of the mass peak and the acoplanarity of the pair. The mass uncertainty of each event is calibrated on the same events, in bins of the predicted uncertainty. Efficiencies. The efficiency of the full lepton selection is measured by tag-and-probe [57] in pseudodata and simulation, with double-sided Crystal Ball function for the signal. The systematic uncertainty is the shift under an alternative signal and background model. Selection. Four-lepton candidates are selected following the criteria of the CMS analysis, requiring recovered final-state radiation, 40 < mZ1 < 120 GeV and 12 < mZ2 < 120 GeV, and kinematic refit of the Z1 mass. The events are split by final state, 4µ, 4e and 2e2µ, and by the relative mass uncertainty. Backgrounds. The background from misidentified leptons is estimated from control regions of the pseudodata, using opposite-sign and same-sign methods and then combining the distributions. The misidentification rates are measured in + ℓ events for light flavor and in eµ + ℓ events for heavy flavor, and the prompt contribution is subtracted. The ZZ backgrounds are taken from simulation, and the normalization of qq ZZ is left free and constrained by control region at 140 < m4ℓ < 165 GeV. Signal model. The signal in each channel is double-sided Crystal Ball function whose shape scales with mH. The cross sections and branching fractions are those of Ref. [70], and the dependence of the acceptance on mH comes from simulation at generator level [35]. Fit. The likelihood is constructed using m4ℓ bins ranging from 105 to 140 GeV with 0.5 GeV width, five bins in the mass uncertainty and three final states, and is maximized using [55]. The mH, µ and the qq ZZ normalization are treated as free parameters in the fit. The nuisance parameters are the lepton scale and resolution, the efficiencies, the misidentified-lepton background, the luminosity and the theory normalizations. The profile likelihood sets the intervals, and their statistical part is obtained with the constrained nuisance parameters fixed. The goodness of fit is taken from pseudoexperiments with saturated-likelihood statistic [52]. Closure. The reference passes closure on the 40 sealed worlds of HIGGSLEPMASS. E.3 LEPCALIB Task. LEPCALIB calibrates the momentum scale, the momentum and angular resolutions, and the identification and trigger efficiencies of and µ. The differences between data and simulation are described by corrections, each function of the lepton kinematics, which analyses apply to simulated events [7274]. In LEPCALIB these corrections themselves are the result. The precision of the lepton calibrations limits that of measurements, and the uncertainty of the lepton momentum scale dominates the systematic uncertainty of the CMS measurement of the Higgs-boson mass in Run-2 [69]. Leptons are calibrated with Z-boson decays. The dilepton mass distribution fixes the momentum scale and resolution, and the tag-and-probe method measures efficiencies [57]. Figure E.3: Expert reference analysis of LEPCALIB on one sealed world: the dimuon mass at the peak before and after the corrections (left) and the momentum-scale correction relative to the injected one (right). The LEPCALIB reference follows the CMS lepton calibrations [57, 7274]. It calibrates each flavor by forward folding and measures the efficiencies with tag-and-probe. Scale and resolution. One opposite-sign pair of identified, isolated leptons per event is used. The simulated leptons are scaled by polynomial in ln pT and η and smeared in pT, η and ϕ by an extra variance per lepton, and the selection is applied after the folding. Simulation and pseudodata are compared in categories of the two leptons. The truncated mean of ln mℓℓ determines the scale and its truncated variance the widths. The ϕ resolution is determined by the shape of the acoplanarity π ϕ at fixed lepton pT. The η resolution is determined for muons by the shape of the η distribution at the edge of the acceptance, and for electrons by the difference between the η of the calorimeter cluster and of the track. single least-squares fit gives scale and widths, with the statistical uncertainty of the simulated templates taken into account. Efficiencies. Tag-and-probe pairs have tag that is identified, isolated and matched to the single-lepton trigger. The efficiencies are measured after the momentum calibration, in bins of pT and η, for each requested identification and trigger leg. The ratio of pseudodata to simulation is described by polynomial in 1/pT and η, fitted to the bins by binomial maximum likelihood. degree is then kept while likelihood-ratio test prefers it at the 5% level, for the scale, the widths and each efficiency. Uncertainties. Each correction has several associated uncertainty sources, which are treated as fully correlated across the kinematic range. The statistical uncertainties of pseudodata and simulation are propagated from the fits. The systematic sources are narrower window and higher tag threshold for the efficiencies, narrower fit windows for the calibration, and for every form the shift to the adjacent degree. Closure. JETCALIB calibrates the energy scale and the energy resolution of jets, hadronic objects that are difficult to handle at the LHC but enter most of its analyses. As in LEPCALIB, the corrections and their uncertainties make up the result. The worlds hold Z( µµ) + jet and multijet events, the latter recorded with prescaled jet triggers. Unlike in LEPCALIB, there is no resonance to calibrate on. The uncertainty of the jet energy scale limits the precision of many measurements. In CMS, the jet energy is corrected in steps, and the residual corrections for the differences between data and simulation are measured in data with the transverse-momentum balance of dijet, + jet and γ + jet events [47]. The pipeline reports the jet energy scale and the jet pT resolution of the pseudodata relative to the simulation, as functions of the jet pT, η and ϕ for pT > 30 GeV and η < 2.5. The balance is biased by additional radiation, by the resolution and by the trigger thresholds, and the forward regions are reached only through the balance of dijet events. The JETCALIB reference follows the CMS calibration [47] in factorized steps. Simulated response. The jets are corrected to the particle level with the response of the simulation, the mean ratio of reconstructed to particle-level pT in slices of η, fitted as function of pT and inverted. The correction is applied to pseudodata and simulation alike. No pileup offset is needed, since pseudodata and simulation share the same pileup. Every change of jet is propagated to the missing transverse momentum. Functional forms. The forms are chosen from the pseudodata. constant is fitted first, and the next polynomial Resolution. The extra resolution is measured from the width of the dijet asymmetry in back-to-back events, in bins of η and of the average pT, with central reference jet for the forward bins. The difference of the squared widths in pseudodata and simulation is extrapolated to no additional jet activity, and fitted in four regions of η, the barrel, two endcap regions and the forward calorimeter. Relative scale. The dependence of the scale on η is measured from the balance of dijet events with the missingtransverse-momentum projection fraction (MPF) method, with central tag jet, as the ratio of pseudodata to simulation extrapolated to no additional jet activity. It is described in each η bin by constant and term in ln pT. Absolute scale. The absolute scale in the central region is obtained from one global fit of the MPF response in Z( µµ)+jet events, the balance of multijet events, which extends the range in pT, and the energy fractions of charged hadrons, neutral hadrons and photons in the jets. The model gives each particle species its own energy scale, linear in ln pT, so that the composition of the jets constrains the dependence of the response on pT. Uncertainties. The statistical uncertainties of pseudodata and simulation are from Poisson bootstrap of the events, with every measurement repeated on each replica. The systematic sources are the choices of the method, namely the extrapolation and the truncation of the asymmetry, the forms of the fits, the propagation of the resolution into the scale, and the dependence of the response on the jet flavor, measured in + jet events. Closure. On the 32 sealed worlds, the reference agrees with the injected truths within its uncertainties. Figure E.4 shows the balance after the corrections on one of them and the scale.
